summary: A young deckhand hangs the ferry's small brass lantern for the first time, on the side the wind comes from, and learns the old custom a visiting sailor taught the pilot. The last crossing ends at the island pier, where the lantern burns and the deckhand dozes under a gray blanket.
source_tradition: Swahili coast, East Africa (dhow sailors' monsoon-wind lore: the kaskazi and kusi winds)
source_note: The monsoon seasons and dhow sailing are traditional, widely documented seafaring knowledge; the lantern custom, characters and wording are entirely original.
hook: Every evening, a small brass lantern is hung on a different side of the Wren Island ferry, and nobody aboard has ever been told why.
context: Fernwick's little green ferry crosses to Wren Island four times a day, and tonight a young deckhand, Joss Penny, hangs the lantern for the first time, learning the custom from the pilot, Barnaby Teague, and the story from the ferry's old cook.

description_summary: The old ferry cook tells why a small brass lantern hangs on a different side of the Fernwick ferry each night, over gentle waves and a soft sea wind.
description_setting: Mid October in Fernwick. The last ferry crosses to Wren Island at dusk, and a young deckhand hangs a brass lantern on the side the wind comes from, an old custom from the Swahili coast of East Africa. The galley smells of ginger biscuits and tea while the waves lap at the hull.
image_brief: A small dark-green ferry resting at a wooden island pier at night: a little brass lantern with thick green glass glowing gold on a hook by the rail, coiled ropes and old tires along the pier, a fogged galley window with warm light and a brown teapot inside, calm black water with soft ripples, one early star and three small yellow windows on the distant island. No faces, no text, no religious symbols.

new_world_facts: The Wren Island ferry is a small, round-shouldered, dark-green boat with a wheelhouse the size of a wardrobe and a galley a little larger.

Dorrit Hale cooked in the ferry's galley for thirty-one years; the galley has four chipped enamel mugs (two blue, two white), a brown teapot with a cracked lid, a lighthouse biscuit tin and a jar of honey.
Hamisi, a sailor from the Swahili coast, spent six wet weeks in Fernwick waiting for an engine part and gave Barnaby Teague a small brass lantern.
The ferry's lantern is hung every evening on the side the wind comes from, so the wind feels welcome; Joss Penny hung it for the first time tonight.
The ferry ties up at the island pier overnight.
script:
[[CHAPTER Welcome]]

Welcome to Fernwick Nights. Tonight's story is The Wind Lantern, told by Dorrit Hale, who cooked in the galley of the Wren Island ferry for thirty-one years. Get comfortable, let the blanket settle, and let the evening slow down.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Lantern]]

Come aboard and sit on the bench by the galley window. I have saved you a cup of tea, and it is still hot. Now, every evening, a small brass lantern is hung on a different side of the Wren Island ferry, and in all my years aboard, nobody was ever told why. The deckhands guessed. The passengers guessed. The gulls, I am quite sure, had opinions. I was only the cook, but cooks hear everything, so I will tell you what I learned, and how I came to learn it.

[pause]

Fernwick is a quiet town on the coast, and its ferry is a small, round-shouldered boat painted dark green, with a wheelhouse the size of a wardrobe and a galley the size of a larger wardrobe. It makes the crossing to Wren Island four times a day. The last one leaves at dusk, when the sky over the water goes the color of a pale plum. Tonight it is mid October, and tonight a young deckhand called Joss Penny is hanging the lantern for the very first time.

[pause]

[[CHAPTER How It Began]]

I should begin with the sailor. Years ago, one wet autumn, a man named Hamisi stayed in Fernwick for six weeks, waiting for a part for his ship's engine to come down the line from the city. He came from the Swahili coast of East Africa, where sailors have crossed the Indian Ocean in wooden boats called dhows for hundreds of years. They had no engines. They used the monsoon winds instead, the kaskazi blowing from the north-east, and the kusi blowing back from the south-west. A good captain, Hamisi told me, knows which wind he is living in the way you know which room of your house you are standing in.

[pause]

The winds, he said, are the calendar of that coast. For half the year one wind blows, and for the other half the other, and a sailor who wants to go home must wait for it to turn, sometimes for months, sitting on a quay with a cup of something hot and watching the sky. Patience, Hamisi said, is the first thing a sailor packs. I thought it was a fine rule for cooks as well.

[pause]

He spent most of those six weeks on our ferry, because it was warm and it smelled of tea. He drank a great deal of it with me, sitting just where you are sitting, with his boots on the rail and his hands wrapped around the cup. The galley was fragrant with ginger biscuits and wet wool, and the stove ticked under the kettle. He taught our pilot, Barnaby Teague, to name the winds, and he taught me to knead a flat bread that puffs up like a small pillow. On his last evening, he gave Barnaby a lantern.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER Which Side]]

It is a plain little thing. The brass has gone the color of old honey, the glass is thick and a little green, and the wick is the width of a bootlace. Hamisi said that sailors on his coast always greet the wind that is going to carry them, and so they hang a light on the side it comes from. The wind sees the light, feels welcome, and takes the boat gently home. It is a very old habit, he said, and a kind one. Barnaby has hung that lantern every evening since, and every evening it goes on a different side, because the wind never comes from the same place twice.

[pause]

Before the last crossing I always set out the same things in the galley. There are four enamel mugs on the shelf, two blue and two white, each with a chip on the rim in a different place. There is the big brown teapot with the cracked lid, a tin of ginger biscuits with a faded picture of a lighthouse, and a jar of honey with a wooden spoon standing in it. The kettle on the stove is already muttering. The window above it has fogged at the corners, so the lights of Harbor Lane look like smudges of butter.

[pause]

So tonight. Joss climbs the steps to the wheelhouse with the lantern held in both hands, as though it were a bowl of soup. The air up there is cool and smells of salt, rope and engine oil. Barnaby is at the wheel, a big, weathered man with a gray cap, and he does not say a word. That is how he teaches. Joss sets the lantern on the shelf, lifts a wet finger to the open window, and holds it still.

[pause]

The cold is on the left side of his finger. A soft, steady breeze is coming from the south-west, over the rail where the afternoon was bright. He thinks about it for a while. Then he lights the wick with a long match, and the little flame stands up straight inside the green glass, small and gold. He carries it down to the deck and hangs it on the hook by the south-west rail. A warm circle of light settles on the boards, on the coiled ropes, on the toes of his boots.

[long pause]

Barnaby, up above, nods once. That is all. Joss feels as though he has been handed a medal.

[pause]

The engine settles into a slow, low hum of its own that comes up through the soles of your feet, and the deck begins to tremble very gently under the boots. The ferry slides away from the Fernwick pier, and the lights of Harbor Lane slip backward one by one, each with its own small gold smear on the water. The tea in the galley is the color of dark amber. Three passengers sit in the cabin: a woman with a basket of eggs, a man with a folded newspaper, and a boy asleep with his chin on his scarf.

[pause]

[[CHAPTER The Crossing]]

Out on the water, the air turns cooler and the swell begins, long and unhurried. It lifts the bow and sets it down again, lift and set, lift and set. Joss stands by the lantern with his back against the cabin wall, watching the flame. It leans a little with each swell and then rights itself. The wind finds it, circles it once, and passes on.

[pause]

In the galley, I slice a loaf into thick, soft pieces and set out the butter. The old saw-edged blade sticks a little, and the loaf is still warm, and the whole room smells of yeast and ginger. I pour a cup for the man with the newspaper. He nods without looking up. The woman with the eggs takes a biscuit and holds it in her hand as though she has forgotten what it is for.

[long pause]

Halfway across, the water goes quiet and black. The sky darkens to the deep blue of the inside of a mussel shell, with one early star in it. Wren Island is a low dark shape ahead, with three small yellow windows. Joss counts the waves quietly to himself, the way Barnaby does, and loses count somewhere past forty, and does not mind.

[pause]

At the island pier, the ferry leans in against the old tires hung along the wood. The engine drops to a murmur. Barnaby brings her round so slowly that the boy in the cabin does not wake. The woman with the eggs steps off with her basket and says, "Goodnight, Joss," and he is so pleased that he forgets to answer.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER Quiet Water]]

The ferry stays at the island pier for the night, tied fore and aft, rocking only a little. Barnaby checks the ropes and goes up to the wheelhouse to write the log in a slow, square hand. I bank the galley stove and wipe the counter with a cloth, and the room settles into a soft orange glow. Joss comes in and sits down on the bench where you are sitting now. He looks a little tired and a little proud.

[pause]

"Why the south-west side?" he asks me, very quietly. I tell him it was the wind's side, and that is the whole of the secret. There is no more to it than that. A light for the wind, so the wind feels welcome. He thinks about this, and then he says it is a lovely thing to do for something you cannot see. I tell him that is exactly what Hamisi said.

[long pause]

Joss thinks of Hamisi, whom he never met, and of the long water far away where the same kind of light has hung from the same kind of rail. He thinks of how many evenings that is, and how many winds. It is too large a number to hold, so he lets it go and watches the flame instead. The glass is warm when he touches it, and the brass is warmer still.

[pause]

The lantern burns on, small and steady, on its hook. Water laps at the hull, a slow, patient sound, like someone turning the pages of a very large book. Out on the deck the boards are cool, and the rope smells of tar and salt. The three yellow windows of the island glow across the water, and the one early star has been joined by several friends.

[pause]

Joss rests his head against the cabin wall. His eyes close and open again. I fetch the gray wool blanket from the locker, the one that smells faintly of cedar, and tuck it around his shoulders. He does not stir. The flame in the green glass leans, rights itself, leans again.

[long pause]

Barnaby comes down at last, puts his cap on the hook, and looks at the sleeping boy for a moment. Then he looks at the lantern. He does not say anything, and neither do I. The wind goes on from the south-west, soft and unhurried, finding its way over the rail and the roof of the galley, out toward the open water and the dark.

[long pause]

[[SECOND]]

[[CHAPTER Once More, Slowly]]

Every evening, a lantern is hung on a different side of the ferry. Nobody ever said why.

[pause]

Joss lifts a wet finger. The wind comes from the south-west. He lights the little flame and hangs it on that side.

[long pause]

The ferry crosses. The water is dark and slow. The island windows glow, and the ferry rests at the pier.

[pause]

A light for the wind, so the wind feels welcome. That is the whole secret.

[long pause]

Joss sleeps under the gray blanket. The lantern burns, small and gold. The water laps, and the wind goes by.

[long pause]

And that is the story of the wind lantern. The tea is still warm, and you can stay on the bench as long as you like. The ferry will keep until morning. Good night.
